name: Path.of()
desc: Builds a file path from parts without hard coding the separator. A Path is an address only; it does not open or create anything.
body:
`Paths.get` does the same job on Java 7 to 10. Use `Path.of` on Java 11 and later.

A relative path is resolved against the directory where `java` was started, not the folder of the source file. When a read fails unexpectedly, print `toAbsolutePath()` before looking for a bug in the code.

name: Files.exists()
desc: Reports whether a path exists. Use it before reading an optional input, not as proof that a later write will succeed.
body: `Files.notExists` is not always the negation: when access is denied, both can return false. For a required input, `Files.exists` followed by a read is the useful pair.

name: Files.createDirectories()
desc: Creates a directory and every missing parent, and does nothing if the directory already exists. Call it before writing into a new folder.
body: `Files.createDirectory` fails when the parent is missing, so it is the wrong call for a nested output folder. `createDirectories` is also safe to call on every run.

name: Files.readAllLines()
desc: Reads a whole text file into a List<String>, one element per line with the terminators removed. Simple and fast for exam sized files.
body: A file with no final newline still yields its last line, and a file ending in a newline does not add an empty element. On a very large file this loads everything into memory; use a `BufferedReader` or `Files.lines` instead.

name: Files.readString()
desc: Reads the whole file into one String, newlines kept. Available since Java 11.
body: Good for a small template or a JSON document that goes to a parser in one piece. To count lines, `lines().count()` or `readAllLines().size()` says it more directly than scanning the string.

name: Files.lines()
desc: Reads a file lazily as a Stream of lines. The stream holds an open file and must be closed.

name: Files.newBufferedReader()
desc: Opens a BufferedReader with a chosen charset. The usual way to read line by line without depending on the platform default encoding.

name: Files.writeString()
desc: Writes one String to a file. Replaces an existing file unless APPEND is passed. Available since Java 11.
body: Default options are `CREATE`, `TRUNCATE_EXISTING`, `WRITE`. Add `StandardOpenOption.APPEND` to keep old content. A missing parent folder still throws `NoSuchFileException`, so create the folder first.

name: Files.write() with a List
desc: Writes an Iterable of lines and puts the platform line separator after each element. Replaces the file by default.
body: The last element also gets a trailing separator, which is fine for CSV and text. Build the list first, then write once; rewriting the file per row is much slower.

name: Files.write() with APPEND
desc: Adds lines to the end of a file instead of replacing it. Pass CREATE as well so the first run can create the file.
body: `APPEND` alone fails with `NoSuchFileException` when the file does not exist yet, and `Files.write` without any option truncates. The pair `CREATE, APPEND` is the one to memorise.

name: Files.newBufferedWriter()
desc: Opens a BufferedWriter with a chosen charset and file options. Use it when many small writes are generated in a loop.

name: Scanner on a file
desc: Reads whitespace separated tokens from a file and converts them with nextInt, nextDouble, or next. Close it when done.
body: `hasNextDouble` stops at a word instead of throwing. The classic trap is mixing `nextInt` with `nextLine`: `nextInt` leaves the newline in the buffer, so the next `nextLine` returns an empty string. Read whole lines and split them when the file has records.

name: StandardCharsets.UTF_8
desc: The charset to pass to every file call that accepts one. Without it, FileReader and FileWriter use the platform default, which can corrupt accented text.
body: Read and write with the same charset. A mismatch does not throw; it silently produces question marks or broken characters. `Files.readAllLines(Path)`, `Files.readString(Path)`, and `Files.newBufferedReader(Path)` already use UTF-8, but the explicit overload documents the intent and survives a JDK change.

name: Files.list()
desc: Lists the entries of one directory as a Stream<Path>. The stream holds a directory handle and must be closed.
body: `Files.walk(dir)` goes into subdirectories and also returns a stream that must be closed. Do not use `File.list()` in new code; it returns null on failure instead of throwing a useful exception.

name: split(",", -1)
desc: Splits a CSV line and keeps trailing empty fields. Without the -1 limit, empty fields at the end disappear and indexes shift.
body:
The first argument is a regex. Escape pipes as `"\\|"` and use `"\\t"` for tabs. The limit `-1` means keep all fields, including empty trailing ones; a positive limit stops after that many fields.

Only trailing empties vanish without the limit. An empty field between two values stays.

name: CSV header to index map
desc: Reads the first line, trims and lowercases each name, and maps a column name to its index. Rows then survive a reordered file.
body:
Check for the columns you need before the loop. A missing key makes `col.get` return null, and unboxing that to an int throws a `NullPointerException` far from the real cause.

If the header starts with `\uFEFF`, a byte order mark from a Windows editor, strip it before splitting.

name: CSV field quoting
desc: Quotes a field only when it contains a comma, a quote, or a line break, and doubles the quotes inside. Required for a CSV that another program can read.
body: A row built with plain `join(",")` breaks on the first city name with a comma. The reader then sees one extra column and every value after it is wrong. Quote on write, and parse quotes on read.

name: CSV parser for quoted fields
syntax: boolean quoted; char by char; "" -> one quote
desc: A small state machine that splits a CSV line while respecting quotes. Handles commas and doubled quotes inside a quoted field.
body: The limit: a quote inside an unquoted value, such as `12" screen`, is treated as an opening quote. Check that the quote starts the field when the data can contain that pattern.

name: Build JSON with StringBuilder
desc: Builds a JSON document without a library. Numbers, booleans, and null go in raw; every string goes through an escaper.
body:
No trailing comma before a closing bracket. Keys are always quoted. A null reference must print `null`, not the four character string `"null"`; the second is a String and a reader will type it as one.

This is fine for a fixed, small object that the program writes. Do not hand parse a document that nests or that someone else produced.

name: JSON string escaping
desc: Escapes the characters that JSON does not allow raw: quote, backslash, newline, carriage return, tab, and control characters below 0x20.
body: Escape the backslash and the quote; the order matters inside the switch because each character is handled once. A name with a quote that is not escaped produces a file that no JSON parser accepts, and the error usually points at the next line.

name: ObjectMapper.readValue()
desc: Deserializes JSON into a class or record. Requires jackson-databind plus core and annotations on the classpath.
body: The class needs a no argument constructor or, on Jackson 2.12 and later, record components that match the JSON keys. Unknown properties throw by default; see the ignore unknown entry. `readValue` also accepts a `String`, an `InputStream`, and a `File`.

name: ObjectMapper.readTree()
desc: Parses JSON into a tree when the shape is unknown or changes between tasks. Read fields with path() and convert with asText, asInt, asBoolean.
body: `asText()` on a number returns its text form, and `asInt()` on a text field parses it when possible. Use `isArray()` before iterating, and `for (JsonNode item : root.path("rooms"))` over an array node.

name: ObjectMapper.writeValueAsString()
desc: Serializes an object or a tree to JSON. Use the pretty printer for a report a human will read, and the plain writer for a compact file.
body: Jackson writes UTF-8 bytes for `writeValue(File, ...)`. `writeValueAsString` returns a String, so write it with an explicit charset. LocalDate fields need the Java time module, or keep dates as String in the DTO.

name: Ignore unknown JSON fields
desc: Stops Jackson from throwing when the JSON has a property the class does not declare. Useful when the input gains fields between tasks.
body: The default is to fail on an unknown property, which is a useful check for a typo in a field name. Turn it off only when the input is outside your control. The annotation version needs `jackson-annotations` on the classpath, which databind already pulls in.
